Choose kNN alone or a fusion configuration
The existing weights and fusion constant are controls to evaluate, not a reason to prefer hybrid on every corpus. Start by checking each input list.
Fusion only reorders the union of its input hits. If a relevant document is missing from every leg, fix retrieval or the embeddings before tuning fusion.

The following requests reuse this recipe's five documents and query vector. Each request goes to POST /helpdesk/_search. The weights 2 and 0.5 and fusion constant 7 are synthetic arithmetic examples, not recommended production settings. They demonstrate the controls, not retrieval quality.
The k inside the knn clause limits that leg's neighbor pool. The k inside the fusion object is the RRF rank constant. The response size controls the final page. These settings do different jobs.

In RRF, a larger weight increases one leg's contribution. A smaller fusion constant gives early ranks more influence relative to deeper ranks. Neither change creates new input hits. A zero weight contributes zero, but a hit returned only by that leg can remain in the union with a zero fused score.
Choose on tuning data, report on held-out data
Prepare representative queries with relevance judgments. Split them into tuning and held-out sets before choosing any settings.

Keep the corpus, judgments, embedder and its version, dimensions, filters, candidate windows and final result cutoff fixed across the four arms. Use the same query vector for each vector-backed request. Record the embedding mode; the lexical default is not a neural model.

On the tuning set, compare kNN alone, equal-weight RRF, weighted RRF and RRF with a custom constant. Choose weights and the constant there, not on the held-out set. Keep the other controls fixed when isolating a weight or constant change.

Evaluate the chosen configurations on the untouched held-out set. Report a relevance metric suited to the task, empty-result rates and relevant documents missing from each leg. Include per-query regressions and uncertainty, not only an average.
Measure latency and cost under the same workload and hardware conditions. Record query time, embedding costs and resource use. A relevance gain may not justify its operational cost.

Prefer kNN alone when it meets your relevance and operational requirements and lexical fusion adds irrelevant hits. Evaluate fusion when lexical hits recover relevant exact terms that the vector leg misses. If the evidence is inconclusive, do not assume the extra configuration helps.

The synthetic corpus above checks request behavior and RRF arithmetic only. It does not select production weights, establish a quality winner, or justify changing the default. The published quality measurements are tied to their stated datasets, embedder and release.

> - **Unknown-field lookups: on `ax-*` (autoindex) indices a wrong field name is a 400, not a silent 0-hit.** Elasticsearch returns `0 hits` for a lookup on an unmapped field, which an agent cannot tell from an empty corpus (measured: 5 of 30 agent intents silently searched a wrong field name). XERJ's wire default is ES's own behaviour — 0 hits — plus an additive `_xerj.hints` `unknown_field` entry naming what does not exist and what does; but the indices `xerj autoindex` creates have full explicit schemas, and there a `term`/`terms`/`match`/`match_phrase`/`match_phrase_prefix`/`prefix`/`wildcard`/`regexp`/`fuzzy`/`range` — or a `multi_match` whose `fields` are ALL unmapped — answers `400` naming the field and the searchable fields (a half-real `multi_match` still searches the real fields, with a hint). On large documents add `"fields":["_passage"]` and project `_source` (see Caveats).

> - **Default `_search` returns whole documents; project `_source` and ask for `_passage` to shrink it.** With no `_source`/`fields` in the request, every hit's `_source` is the complete stored document — for source files or long documents that is megabyte-scale for a handful of hits (measured: 5 hits over indexed source files = 416,630 bytes). Add `"fields":["_passage"]` to any query (lexical, or a single semantic/kNN clause — omit it for hybrid/multi-kNN fusion, which 400s naming the fix) to get just the matching snippet — `{field,ordinal,start_offset,end_offset,text,page?}` sliced from the original field — and project `_source` (e.g. `["title","ax_path"]`, or `false`) to drop the rest: the same query measured 12,122 bytes that way, a 34× reduction. `_passage` is opt-in and appears in no `_mapping` or default response, so a response that would benefit says so itself — an additive `_xerj.hints` entry carrying a ready-to-send corrected request can land ahead of `hits` when `_source` is unprojected and `_passage` wasn't requested (not on every response: a one-record JSONL hit on rc.101 carried none; it is for responses that are large without it) (never inside `hits`/`total`/`_score`, so existing ES clients are unaffected).
